title: The `if` statement executes the code inside it only when the condition is True.
when_to_show: When determining which line is executed in an `if` statement
body: An `if` statement executes the indented code inside it only when the result of the conditional expression is `True`. A comparison expression such as `score >= 60` evaluates to either `True` or `False`, and that result determines the flow of execution. If the condition is `False`, the indented block following the `if` statement is skipped. Therefore, when reading an `if` problem, you must first check the variable values and use those values to determine whether the conditional expression is true or false. When analyzing this concept, rather than simply focusing on getting the correct answer, you should systematically verify which lines set the values and which lines evaluate the conditions or determine the execution path. Beginners tend to simply memorize the results of `if` statements or lists, but when actually reading code, you must track the truth value of the conditional expression, the scope of indentation, and the current state of the list all at once. This card focuses on using small examples to help you reliably read the decision flows that repeatedly appear in real-world code. An `if` statement executes the code inside it only when the condition is `True`. You must first determine whether the conditional expression is a comparison operator, a variable itself, or the result of a function call. If a value changes inside the `if` block, the results of subsequent lines may also change. Conversely, if the condition is False, the inner lines are skipped, so any assignments or outputs on those lines do not occur.
detail: When reading an `if` statement, you first determine whether the condition is `True` or `False`, and then decide whether the indented lines inside the block will be executed. If the condition is `False`, the assignment or output inside the block does not occur. To accurately predict the subsequent results, you must also track whether the variable’s value has changed in the preceding line or is changed again within the `if` block.

title: The `else` clause is the alternative path that is executed when the `if` condition is false.
when_to_show: When choosing which of the two branches of an if/else statement to execute
body: The `else` block is an alternative path that executes when the `if` condition is `False`. If the `if` condition is `True`, the `if` block is executed and the `else` block is skipped. Conversely, if the `if` condition is `False`, the `if` block is not executed and the `else` block is executed. When reading code, you must not assume that both blocks will be executed. You should interpret the structure as one where only one path is chosen based on the condition’s value. When analyzing this concept, rather than simply focusing on getting the correct answer, you should systematically verify which line determines the value and which line evaluates the condition or position. Beginners often tend to simply memorize the results of `if` statements or lists, but in actual code reading, you must track the truth value of the conditional expression, the scope of indentation, and the current state of the list simultaneously. This card focuses on reliably reading the decision flow that repeatedly appears in real-world code through small examples. The `else` block is an alternative path that executes when the `if` condition is `False`. The code inside the `if` block and the code inside the `else` block do not execute simultaneously. When reading code, you must first determine whether the conditional expression is `True` or `False`, and then follow only the selected block. If you misinterpret the indentation scope, it’s easy to get confused about which lines are executed.
detail: An `if/else` statement is a structure that selects only one of two paths. If the `if` condition is `True`, only the `if` block is executed; if it is `False`, only the `else` block is executed. It’s easy to get the result wrong if you assume that both blocks are executed. When reading code, break it down into the following steps in order: evaluating the conditional expression, the indented block that is selected, and the common flow following that block.

title: Comparison operators return True or False.
when_to_show: When reading the meanings of comparison operators such as ==, !=, >, and >=
body: Comparison operators compare two values to return True or False. == checks if the values are equal, and != checks if they are not equal. >= checks if the value on the left is greater than or equal to the value on the right. Since = is an assignment operator that stores a value, and == is a comparison operator that compares values, it is essential to distinguish between the two. In conditional statements, the result of these comparisons determines whether the code is executed. When reading this concept, rather than just focusing on getting the correct answer, you should check step by step which line sets the value and which line evaluates the condition or position. Beginners tend to memorize only the results of `if` statements or lists, but when actually reading code, they must track the truth value of the conditional expression, the scope of indentation, and the current state of the list simultaneously. This card focuses on using small examples to help you reliably read the decision flows that repeatedly appear in real-world code. Comparison operators compare two values to produce True or False. == checks for equality, != checks for inequality, and < and > check for size relationships. When you see a comparison expression inside a conditional statement, you must first identify the left and right values. The meaning can vary depending on whether it’s a numeric or string comparison, and the code inside the if statement is executed only when the comparison result is True.
detail: Comparison operators compare two values and return either True or False. It is important to distinguish between `==`, which checks for equality, and `=`, which is an assignment operator used to store a value. When a comparison expression appears within a conditional statement, the left-hand and right-hand values are evaluated first; after determining whether the comparison is between numbers or strings, the block of code to be executed is determined.

title: An empty string and an empty list are treated as "False" in conditional statements.
when_to_show: When reading code that uses values themselves as conditions, such as `if text` or `if items`,
body: A condition evaluates an object's truth value. None, False, numeric zero, empty strings, and empty containers are false; most non-empty containers are true. A custom object can change the rule with __bool__ or __len__, so do not generalize this as 'anything with a value is true.'
detail: A condition evaluates an object's truth value. None, False, numeric zero, empty strings, and empty containers are false; most non-empty containers are true. A custom object can change the rule with __bool__ or __len__, so do not generalize this as 'anything with a value is true.'

title: List indices start at 0.
when_to_show: When reading code that retrieves values by index, such as `items[0]` and `items[1]`
body: A list index is a way to retrieve values from a list by their position, and in Python, it starts at 0. If `items = ["A", "B", "C"]`, then `items[0]` is "A", `items[1]` is "B", and `items[2]` is "C". The most important point is that the first value is at index 0, not 1. `len(items)` returns the number of elements in the list. If the length is 3, the valid positive indices are 0, 1, and 2. Therefore, the position of the last element is usually calculated as `len(items) - 1`. If you use the length value directly as an index, such as `items[len(items)]`, you may go out of bounds. This distinction appears very frequently in beginner-level problems. When reading code, it’s safest to first write down the current contents of the list and indicate which value each index points to. If `append`, `pop`, or index assignment operations were performed earlier, the list’s length or element positions may have changed. When iterating directly over the index in a loop—such as `for i in range(len(items))`—you must also track the range over which the value of `i` changes, starting from 0. Understanding negative indices also makes reading lists easier. `items[-1]` refers to the last element, and `items[-2]` refers to the second-to-last element. However, for beginner-level problems, it’s important to first gain a solid understanding of the relationship between positive indices and `len`. Indexing errors mostly occur when trying to retrieve a value from an empty list or when confusing the list’s length with the last position. For example, in a list of length 3, `items[3]` attempts to access the fourth position, resulting in an error. To access elements safely, you should always compare the current length of the list with the index you’re trying to access. Additionally, it’s helpful to distinguish between slicing and indexing. While `items[1]` retrieves a single value, `items[1:3]` creates a new list containing multiple values. At the beginner level, first check whether there is a single number or a colon inside the square brackets. A single number indicates positional access, while a colon indicates range access. When solving indexing problems, writing down the list’s current state, the position you’re trying to access, and the result’s data type can help reduce mistakes.
detail: Since list indices start at 0, only positions 0, 1, and 2 are safe in a list of length 3. items[len(items)] is prone to out-of-bounds errors, and the last value is typically accessed as items[-1] or items[len(items)-1]. When reading code, compare the list’s current contents, its length, and the index you’re trying to access.

title: append() adds a value to the end of a list
when_to_show: When tracking how the state changes after a value is added to the list
body: `append()` is a method that adds a single value to the end of a list. If you execute `items.append('A')` after `items = []`, `items` becomes `['A']`. If `append` is called multiple times, the values are appended in the order they were called. When solving output problems, it’s safest to write down the current state of the list each time you encounter an `append` line. When reading this concept, rather than just focusing on getting the correct answer, you should check step by step which lines set values and which lines evaluate conditions or determine positions. Beginners often tend to memorize only the results of `if` statements or lists, but when actually reading code, you must track the truth values of conditional expressions, the scope of indentation, and the current state of the list simultaneously. This card focuses on reliably reading the decision flows that repeatedly appear in real-world code through small examples. `append` adds a single value to the end of a list. If `append` appears inside a loop, it’s highly likely that values are being accumulated sequentially. When reading code, you must verify whether the values being appended are the original values, calculated values, or values that have passed a condition. It’s helpful to write down the final shape of the list after the loop.
detail: The `append` method adds a single value to the end of the list and directly modifies the list’s state. If `append` is used inside a loop, values are added sequentially each time the loop iterates. When reading code, it’s a good idea to check whether the value being appended is the original value, the result of a calculation, or a value that passed a condition, and to note the state of the list after each iteration.

title: len() counts the number of elements in a list
when_to_show: When checking the length of a list after an `append` operation or determining whether a list is empty
body: len() is a function that counts the number of values in a list and returns an integer. The length of an empty list [] is 0, and the length of ["A", "B"] is 2. len(items) does not print the list itself; instead, it returns the number of elements. Therefore, it is frequently used in comparisons, loops, and conditional expressions. Since lists are mutable, the result of `len` may change if operations such as `append`, `pop`, `remove`, or index assignment are executed beforehand. `append` typically increases the length by 1, while `pop` typically decreases the length by 1. Simply looking at the initial list to choose an answer may lead to an incorrect result, so you must check the state of the list at the time `len` is executed. The relationship between indices and length is also important. For a list of length 4, the last positive index is 3, not 4. Therefore, when calculating the last position, `len(items) - 1` is often used. Conversely, if the list is empty, `len(items)` is 0, and `items[0]` cannot be used. When reading code, you should distinguish whether the result of `len` is stored in a variable, used in a conditional comparison, or used with `range` to determine the number of iterations. `len` is also frequently used when creating loop conditions. `for i in range(len(items))` causes `i` to iterate from 0 to `len(items)-1`, so you can use each `i` as an index to retrieve `items[i]`. However, if you only need the values themselves, `for item in items` is simpler. When reading code that uses `len`, you should check whether an index is required. There is also code that loops until the list is empty, such as `while len(items) > 0:`. In such cases, you must verify whether `pop` or `remove` is executed within the loop, causing the length to decrease, to avoid infinite loops or errors.
detail: `len` returns the number of elements in a list. If the list has been modified using `append` or `pop`, the result of `len` will also change. Since length and index are different, if the length is 4, the last positive index is 3. You should read the code carefully to distinguish whether `len` is being used for conditional checks, `range` loops, or checking for an empty list.

title: A list allows you to change the value at a specific position.
when_to_show: When reading code that modifies values within a list, such as `items[0] = 'Z'`
body: A list is a mutable data type, meaning its internal values can be changed even after it has been created. `items[0] = "Z"` does not create a new variable named `items`; instead, it changes the value at index 0 of the list that `items` points to. Therefore, when you print `items` on the next line, you will see the updated value. When reading a list modification problem, you must check both which position has changed and what element was actually at that position. Since indices start at 0, `items[1]` refers to the second value. `append` adds a new value to the end of the list, while `pop` removes a value from the list by extracting it. Index assignment replaces the existing value at a specific position with a different value. Another important point is that multiple variables can point to the same list. If you assign a = items and then execute a[0] = "X," the list that appears to be `items` may also seem to have changed. This is because, in reality, `a` and `items` were both referencing the same list object. When solving problems, writing out the entire contents of the list after each line allows you to safely track the flow of mutations. List mutations are particularly important in debugging. If a function takes a list as an argument and sorts it or adds values internally, the list passed to the function may also be affected. Therefore, when you need to preserve the original, you should create a copy and work on that instead. Additionally, if you modify the same list while iterating over it with a `for` loop, you may get unexpected results. At the beginner level, it’s a good habit to rewrite the entire list each time a line of code is executed. By observing in sequence what values `items` point to, how the internal elements change, and what state the list is in at the time of output, you can significantly reduce errors.
detail: A list is a mutable data type whose internal values can be changed. `items[0] = 'Z'` does not create a new variable; rather, it changes the value at index 0 of the same list. If multiple variables point to the same list, changes made in one place may be reflected in the other names as well; therefore, you must track the entire state of the list after each line.
